svg.text: How a macrophage destroys what it engulfs
Phagocytosis, lysosomal biogenesis and vesicular trafficking, and what happens when particles cannot be cleared

text.tspan: Tissue-resident phagocytes of the innate immune system
Live in the alveolar lumen, on the epithelium, bathed in surfactant-rich lining
fluid
Clear microbes, dust and dead cells; their cytokines alert other immune cells
Opsonins (IgG, iC3b) bridge bacterium and receptor; FcγR, CR3 and the mannose
receptor trigger uptake. TLR4 senses LPS and only signals. CR1 binds C3b/C4b.
Branched F-actin pushes pseudopods around the particle (2.2, the cup in the
cell) until the membrane seals into a phagosome (2.3).
Inhaled particles reach the alveoli, where macrophages take
them up but cannot digest them.
Pseudopods spread along a fibre too long to enclose, but the cup
never closes: ROS and lysosomal enzymes leak out. Short fibres
can be engulfed yet still persist.
Crystals can rupture the phagolysosome membrane. Leaked
cathepsins, K⁺ efflux and ROS can activate the NLRP3
inflammasome → caspase-1 → IL-1β. Cells that die release the
crystal, which is engulfed again.
Signalling: IL-1β, TNF-α and
chemokines recruit neutrophils and
monocytes.
Injury: their ROS and proteases
damage the epithelium; the particle
stays.
Myofibroblasts deposit collagen: septa thicken and stiffen, air
spaces shrink and gas exchange fails.
Steps 2.1 → 2.6 happen in sequence, while the enzyme route 3.1 → 3.6 runs continuously
alongside them.

svg.text: magnified at 4: a lysosome meets the late phagosome

text.tspan: a Tethering. Rab7-GTP recruits the HOPS
complex, which bridges both membranes
b Zipping. Syntaxin-7, Vti1b and syntaxin-8
coil with VAMP7
c Fusion. A pore opens and contents mix; NSF
later recycles the SNAREs

svg.text: step 2.7: two separate mechanisms, magnified from 2.3–2.6

text.tspan: Oxidative burst (from 2.3): NOX2 passes
electrons from cytosolic NADPH to O₂ →
superoxide → H₂O₂
Acid hydrolysis (after fusion, 2.6): V-ATPase
pumps H⁺ in; cathepsins, lipases, nucleases and
glycosidases dismantle the bacterium
Products (amino acids, sugars, nucleotides) leave for reuse; some peptides are presented on MHC II to T cells.
Clearing a microbe needs two routes to converge: the maturing
phagosome and lysosomal enzyme delivery. When the cargo
cannot be degraded, the same machinery drives lung injury.
